text:
Installing and loading packages
Just like every other programming language you may be familiar with, R’s capabilities can be greatly extended by installing additional “packages” and “libraries”.
To install a package, use the install.packages() command. You’ll want to run the following commands to get the necessary packages for today’s lab:
install.packages("rmdformats")
install.packages("ggplot2")
install.packages("knitr")
You only need to install packages once. Once they’re installed, you may use them by loading the libraries using the library() command. For today’s lab, you’ll want to run the following code

library(knitr)   # contains kable() function

text:
In-Class Exercise: Indexing

How to use indexing to get the midterm grade of Noah?
How to get the students name with midterm grade above 90?
If the weight changes to 30% for midterm and 70% for final, only the students whose grade greater than or equal to 90 will get an A. Who will get an A in this course?


Functions on vectors







Command
Description




sum(vec)
sums up all the elements of vec


mean(vec)
mean of vec


median(vec)
median of vec


min(vec), max(vec)
the largest or smallest element of vec


sd(vec), var(vec)
the standard deviation and variance of vec


length(vec)
the number of elements in vec


pmax(vec1, vec2), pmin(vec1, vec2)
example: pmax(quiz1, quiz2) returns the higher of quiz 1 and quiz 2 for each student


sort(vec)
returns the vec in sorted order


order(vec)
returns the index that sorts the vector vec


unique(vec)
lists the unique elements of vec


summary(vec)
gives a five-number summary


any(vec), all(vec)
useful on Boolean vectors




Example


course_grades

[1] 78.8 86.4 94.2 82.0 92.6

mean(course_grades) # mean grade

[1] 86.8

median(course_grades)

[1] 86.4

sd(course_grades) # grade standard deviation

[1] 6.625708

sort(course_grades)

[1] 78.8 82.0 86.4 92.6 94.2

max(course_grades) # highest course grade

[1] 94.2

min(course_grades) # lowest course grade

[1] 78.8




Pairwise comparisons
Is the final score higher than the midterm score?

midterm 

[1] 80 90 93 82 95

final

[1] 78 84 95 82 91

final > midterm

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE


Boolean operators can be applied elementwise:

(final < midterm) & (midterm > 80)

[1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE  TRUE


Note: The logical operator && and || considers only the first element of the vectors and give a vector of single element as output.


More referencing
which() returns the TRUE indexes of a Boolean vector:

course_grades

[1] 78.8 86.4 94.2 82.0 92.6

a_threshold <- 90 # A grade = 90% or higher
course_grades >= a_threshold # vector of booleans

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE

a_students <- which(course_grades >= a_threshold) # Applying which() 
a_students

[1] 3 5

students_name[a_students] # Names of A students

[1] "Sarah"  "Joseph"


A different way to solve it

students_name[course_grades >= a_threshold]

[1] "Sarah"  "Joseph"

title: Interlude: Intro to R, RStudio, Markdown
text:
Matrices
A matrix is a two-dimensional rectangular data set. It can be created using a vector input to the matrix function.

# Create a matrix.
M = matrix( c('a','a','b','c','b','a'), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
print(M)

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,] "a"  "a"  "b" 
[2,] "c"  "b"  "a" 


Is there any difference if we choose FALSE for byrow?

# Create a different matrix.
M = matrix( c('a','a','b','c','b','a'), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = FALSE)
print(M)

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,] "a"  "b"  "b" 
[2,] "a"  "c"  "a" 


How to access each element?

M[1,2] # The first row and the second column

[1] "b"

title: Interlude: Intro to R, RStudio, Markdown
text:
Factors
Factors are the r-objects which are created using a vector. It stores the vector along with the distinct values of the elements in the vector as labels. The labels are always character irrespective of whether it is numeric or character or Boolean etc. in the input vector. They are useful in statistical modeling.
Factors are created using the factor() function. The nlevels functions gives the count of levels.

# Create a vector.
apple_colors <- c('green','green','yellow','red','red','red','green')

# Create a factor object.
factor_apple <- factor(apple_colors)

# Print the factor.
print(factor_apple)

[1] green  green  yellow red    red    red    green 
Levels: green red yellow

print(nlevels(factor_apple))

[1] 3


We can also use as.factor() to convert a numeric vector to a factor

numbers <- c(1,1,2,3,2,1,2)
print(numbers)

[1] 1 1 2 3 2 1 2

print(class(numbers))

[1] "numeric"

print(as.factor(numbers))

[1] 1 1 2 3 2 1 2
Levels: 1 2 3

print(class(as.factor(numbers)))

[1] "factor"


Note: Some class labels are stored as numeric. However, if you want to do classification, you need to convert it to a factor.

title: Interlude: Intro to R, RStudio, Markdown
text:
Data Frames
Data frames are tabular data objects. Unlike a matrix in data frame each column can contain different modes of data. The first column can be numeric while the second column can be character and third column can be logical. It is a list of vectors of equal length.
Data Frames are created using the data.frame() function.

BMI <-  data.frame(
   gender = c("Male", "Male","Female"), 
   height = c(152, 171.5, 165), 
   weight = c(81,93, 78),
   Age = c(42,38,26)
)
print(BMI)

  gender height weight Age
1   Male  152.0     81  42
2   Male  171.5     93  38
3 Female  165.0     78  26


How to access each column/attribute? How to access each row/observation?

BMI$height # to access height

[1] 152.0 171.5 165.0

BMI[,2] # a different way to access height

[1] 152.0 171.5 165.0

BMI[2,] # to access the second row

  gender height weight Age
2   Male  171.5     93  38

title: Week 2:Introduction to Statistics and Descriptive Statistics
text:
Introduction to Statistics

What is statistics?
Statistics is the study of the collection, organization, analysis, and interpretation of data.
Basics of statistics:

Population: the entire group of individuals that we want information about.
Sample: a part of the population that we actually examine in order to gather information about the whole population.


Example:
Population: Illinois Tech students Sample: Students in our class

Types of statistics:

Descriptive statistics: utilizes numerical and graphical methods to look for patterns in a data set, to summarize the information revealed in a data set, and to present the information in a convenient form.
Inferential statistics: use a fact about a sample to estimate the truth about the whole population.













Descriptive Statistics
General two types of data:

Qualitative data: observations that cannot be measured on a numerical scale. They can only be classified into one of a group of categories.
Example: species of fish, eye color, marital status etc.
Quantitative data: measurements that are recorded on a naturally occurring numerical scale.
Example: height of person, score of test, etc.


Numerical Methods
Consider a quantitative dataset with \(n\) observations, denoted as \(\{x_1,\cdots,x_n\}\).

Location Measures

Sample Mean: arithmetic average, denoted by \(\bar{x}\)
\[\bar{x} = \frac{x_1+\cdots+x_n}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n x_i=\frac{1}{n}\sum x_i\]

The corresponding population parameter is population mean, denoted by \(\mu\).

Sample median: middle number when the observations are arranged in ascending order, noted by \(\tilde{x}\)

\[\tilde{x} = \begin{cases} x_{(n+1)/2}, & \text{ if } n \text{ is odd,} \\
      \frac{1}{2}(x_{n/2} + x_{n/2+1}), & \text{ if } n \text{ is even.} \end{cases}
      \]

Note: Median is less sensitive than mean to extremely large or small observations, which is good.
For example, a dataset \(\{-3,0,4\}\), the sample mean is \(1/3\) and the sample median is \(0\).
If the observation 4 is changed to 18, then the sample mean becomes \(5\), while the sample median stays unchanged as \(0\).

Variability Measures

Sample range: measure of variability, \(x_{\max} -x_{\min}\)
Sample variance: measure of variability, spread out, denoted by \(s^2\)


\[ s^2 = \frac{(x_1-\bar{x})^2+\cdots+(x_n-\bar{x})^2}{n-1} = \frac{\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar{x})^2}{n-1} \]
The corresponding population parameter is population variance, denoted as $\sigma^2$.

Sample standard deviation: \(s = \sqrt{s^2}\), common way for measuring how far observations are away from the mean.
The corresponding population parameter is the population standard deviation, denoted as \(\sigma\).

Example 1. Consider a tiny data set with three observations 5, 0, and 1. Find the sample mean, sample median, sample variance, and sample standard deviation.
\(\bar{x} = (0+1+5)/3 = 2\), \(\tilde{x} = 1\),
\[s^2 = \frac{1}{3-1}\left[(0-2)^2+(1-2)^2
+(5-2)^2\right] = \frac{4+1+9}{3-1} = 7,\qquad s = \sqrt{7}.\]

title: Week 3: Normal Distributions
text:
Normal Distribution
The normal distribution (also be called Gaussian distribution) is a symmetric distribution that is centered around a mean and spreads out in both directions.
Examples: Test scores for all ITMS 514 students.

Notation: \(X\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\)

\(\mu\) is the mean of the distribution
\(\sigma^2\) is the variance of the distribution

X can take any value on the real line.
Areas under the Normal Curve:

\[\begin{align*}
F(x) &=P(X<x) = P(X \le x) \\
F(x_2) -F(x_1) =P(x_1<X<x_2)= &P(x_1\le X<x_2)= P(x_1<X\le x_2) = P(x_1 \le X \le x_2).
\end{align*}\]
Suppose \(Z\) is the standard normal random variable, i.e., \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\)










Different Normal Distributions

Same Mean but Different Variances










-Different Means and Variances











Calculate the probability for the Normal Distribution
Question: What’s the relationship between the general normal random variable \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) and the standard normal random variable?
\[Z= \frac{X-\mu}{\sigma} \sim N(0,1).\]
To calculate the probability involving \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\),
\[
    P(a\leq X\leq b) = P\left(\frac{a-\mu}{\sigma}\leq \frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\leq \frac{b-\mu}{\sigma}\right)
    = P\left(\frac{a-\mu}{\sigma}\leq Z\leq \frac{b-\mu}{\sigma}\right),
\]
Example 1: The achievement scores from a college entrance examination are normally distributed with mean 75 and standard deviation 10. What fraction of the scores lies between 80 and 90?
Answer: The scores \(X\sim N(75,10^2)\), then \[P(80\leq X\leq 90) = P\left(\frac{80-75}{10}\leq Z\leq \frac{90-75}{10}\right) = P(0.5\leq Z\leq 1.5) .\] How to get the answer in R?

p1 # display the answer

p2<-pnorm(90, mean = 75, sd =10) -pnorm(80, mean = 75, sd =10) # find the P(80 <=X <=90)
p2 # display the answer

Critical value: \(z_{\alpha}\) of a standard normal distribution is the value on the measurement axis for which \(\alpha\) of the area under the standard normal curve lies to the right of \(z_{\alpha}\).

title: Week 3: Special Discrete Random Distributions
text:
Special Discrete Distributions
Bernoulli and Binomial distributions are related to experiments with binary outcome (success or failure).

Bernoulli Distribution
Bernoulli Trial: A single random experiment with outcome either success or failure, and the probability of the success is \(p\).
Examples - Flip a single coin - Shot a free throw
Bernoulli Random Variable: A random variable that takes either \(1\) or \(0\), where it takes 1 when the outcome of the Bernoulli trial is a success and 0 when the outcome of the Bernoulli trial is a failure.
Bernoulli Distribution: The distribution of a Bernoulli random variable is called the Bernoulli distribution.
Notation: \(X\sim Bernoulli(p)\)
PMF of Bernoulli Distribution/Random Variable:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
x & 0 & 1 \\
\hline
P(X = x) & 1-p & p  \\
\end{array}
\]
Expectation and Variance
\[E(X) = (0)(1-p)+(1)p = p,\qquad var(X) = (0)^2(1-p)+(1)^2p -p^2 = p(1-p)\]


Investigate \(p\) via Tossing Coin Experiments
Suppose we have a fair coin and consider head as a success. Thus \(p = 0.5\). We generate 10 instances from the Bernoulli distribution.

# number of random experiments
n <- 10
# sample space for tossing a coin, 0--Tail, 1--Head
x <- c(0,1)
# generate n outcomes of the experiments
coinToss <- sample(x, size=n, replace=TRUE)
# display the results
coinToss

 [1] 0 1 1 0 0 0 1 1 0 0


We can use bar plot to show the frequency of each value in a categorical/discrete variable.

barplot(table(coinToss))








This is actually a sample from the distribution with sample size 10. Let’s investigate the sample mean.

phat <- mean(coinToss)
phat

[1] 0.4


Question: What happened if we increase the sample size?
Let \(n =100\)

# number of random experiments
n <- 100 
# sample space for tossing a coin, 0--Tail, 1--Head
x <- c(0,1) 
# generate n outcomes of the experiments
coinToss <- sample(x, size=n, replace=TRUE)
# display the results
barplot(table(coinToss))







phat <- mean(coinToss)
phat

[1] 0.45


Let’s try \(n = 10,000\).

# number of random experiments
n <- 10000
# sample space for tossing a coin, 0--Tail, 1--Head
x <- c(0,1) 
# generate n outcomes of the experiments
coinToss <- sample(x, size=n, replace=TRUE)
# display the results
barplot(table(coinToss))







phat <- mean(coinToss)
phat

[1] 0.4988


Question: What can we learn from the experiment?
Conclusion: Given a sample of independent and identically distributed (IID) values, the sample mean converges to the expectation (true/population mean).


Binomial Distribution
Binomial Trial: Repeat Bernoulli trial independently for a certain number (\(n\)) of times, each repetition has the same possible outcomes (success or failure), and the probability of each success (\(p\)) is consistent for all trials. This experiment is called Binomial trial.
Binomial Random Variable: The number of successes \(X\) of a binomial trial is called a Binomial random variable.
Binomial Distribution: The distribution of a Binomial random variable is called the binomial distribution
Examples:

Number of heads in 40 coin flips
Number of hits in 20 free throws

Notation: \(X\sim B(n,p)\), \(n\) is the number of Bernoulli trials and \(p\) is the probability of success in each trial.
PMF: \(b(x;n,p) = {n\choose x}p^x(1-p)^{n-x}\), \(x=0,1,\ldots,n\)
Mathematical Reason: \(f(x) = P(X=x)\), that is, in \(n\) trials, we observe \(x\) successes. The probability of an outcome with \(x\) successes is \(p^x(1-p)^{n-x}\) (the trials are independent). The number of such outcomes is: \({n\choose x}\) (choosing \(x\) trials for success in \(n\) trials).
Expectation and Variance: \[E(X) = np, \qquad var(X) = np(1-p).\] Binomial random variable \(X\sim B(n,p)\) can be viewed as the sum of \(n\) independent and identical Bernoulli random variables, i.e., \[X = Y_1+\cdots+Y_n,\] where \(X\sim B(n,p)\), \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\sim Bernoulli(p)\) and \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) are independent. Thus, by the properties of expected value and variance, \[\begin{align*}
E(X) & = E(Y_1+\cdots+Y_n) = E(Y_1)+\cdots+E(Y_n) = np,\\
var(X) &= var(Y_1+\cdots+Y_n) = var(Y_1)+\cdots+var(Y_n) = np(1-p).
\end{align*}\]

title: Week3: Introduction to Random Variables
text:
Random Variable
Variable: A variable is a quantity that may change within the context of a mathematical problem or experiment.
Random Variable: A random variable is a numerical description of the outcome of an experiment.
Examples:

\(X =\) number of heads after tossing a fair coin 100 times.
\(Y =\) number of 6s after rolling a fair die 100 times.
\(Z =\) number of As in this class.
\(A =\) amount of time you spent watching TV every week.


Types of Random Variables:

Discrete random variable: take on a finite (or countable) number of values.
Examples:

Sum of two dice: \(\{2, 3, 4,\ldots, 12\}\).
Number of children: \(\{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}\).

Continuous random variables: take on values in a continuum (usually an interval)。
Examples:

Height: \((0,2.5)\) meters
Weight: \((0,200)\) pounds
Time: \((0,75)\) minutes




Describe a Discrete Random Variable
Tossing Coin Experiment: Toss a fair coin 3 times. Suppose we are interested in the random variable \(X =\) number of heads.How do we get the probabilities??
We know the total number of outcomes of this experiment is \(2^3 = 8\). Why?

\(X=0\), i.e., \(P(X=0)  = P(\{TTT\}) = 1/8 = \frac{1}{8};\)
\(X=1\), i.e., \(P(X=1)  = P(\{HTT\})+P(\{THT\})+P(\{TTH\}) = \frac{3}{8};\)
\(X =2\), i.e., \(P(X=2)  =P(\{HHT\})+P(\{HTH\})+P(\{THH\})  = \frac{3}{8};\)
\(X =3\), i.e., \(P(X=3)  = P(\{HHH\}) = \frac{1}{8}\)

Thus, we can have the following table \[\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3  \\
\hline
P(X = x) & \frac{1}{8} & \frac{3}{8} & \frac{3}{8} & \frac{1}{8}
\end{array}\]

Using R to simulate this random variable
We can use sample function to generate an observation of this random variable

n <- 3
x <- c(0,1)
#1 indicates Head 0 indicate Tail
sample(x, size=n, replace=TRUE) #simulate flipping coin 3 times

[1] 1 0 1

# Here X1 is one observation
X1<- sum(sample(x, size=n, replace=TRUE)) 
X1

[1] 1

# Here X2 is another observation
X2<- sum(sample(x, size=n, replace=TRUE)) 
X2

[1] 2




PMF and Its Properties
PMF(Probability Mass Function): The values on the right of the table above are called the Probability Mass Function of the random variable \(X\).

\(f(x)\geq 0\) for all \(x\in R\). (PMFs are non-negative)
There are only finitely (or countably infinitely many) \(x\)’s for which \(f(x) > 0\). (The probability of other values are 0.)
\(\sum\limits_x f(x) = 1\). (The sum of probabilities over all possible values is 1.)
\(P(X = x) = f(x)\).

The following table is the PMF for \(X\), the number of heads tossing a fair coin 3 times. \[\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3  \\
\hline
P(X = x) & \frac{1}{8} & \frac{3}{8} & \frac{3}{8} & \frac{1}{8}
\end{array}\]
Let’s generate a sample with size 10 of this random variable.

resultOf10rep<-replicate(10, sum(sample(x, size=n, replace=TRUE)))
resultOf10rep 

 [1] 2 2 2 3 2 1 1 2 2 2

replicate(10, sum(sample(x, size=n, replace=TRUE)))

 [1] 0 2 2 1 2 2 2 1 1 1


CDF(Cumulative Distribution Function): \(F(x)\) of a random variable \(X\) with PMF \(f(x)\) is \[ F(x) = P(X \le x ) = \sum_{t \le x } f(t), \qquad -\infty <x <\infty. \]
Example: CDF of \(X\), the number of heads tossing a fair coin 3 times \[F(x) =
\begin{cases}
0 & x < 0\\
\frac{1}{8} &  x < 1 \\
\frac{1}{2} & x < 2\\
\frac{7}{8} & x <3 \\
1 & x \ge 3
\end{cases}.\]



Expected Value of a Discrete Random Variable or a Function of a Discrete Random Variable

Expected Value (Population Mean) of a Discrete Random Variable
Expected value: The expected value of a random variable \(X\) with PMF \(f(x)\) is given by: \[\mu = E(X) =  \sum_x xf(x).\]

The expected value is a weighted average of the possible values of \(X\), weighted by the probabilities. We may interchangeably use population mean or mean, average, expectation, and expected value, and the notations \(E(X)\) or \(\mu\).
The expected value of a random variable can be understood as the long-run average value of the random variable in repeated independent trials.

Example: Expectation of \(X\), the number of heads tossing a fair coin 3 times is
\[\begin{align*}
    \mu =E(X) & = \sum_x xf(x) = 0\cdot \frac{1}{8} + 1 \cdot \frac{3}{8} + 2\cdot \frac{3}{8} + 3\cdot \frac{1}{8} = \frac{3}{2}.
\end{align*}\]
This means, if we perform the experiment many many many times, and each time we record the value of \(X\) , then the average value of these observed \(X\) values is approximately 3/2. If we can perform the experiment infinitely many times, then the average value will be exactly 3/2.


Using R to generate samples with different sizes and calculate the sample mean
Recall the experiment we did, what value is the sample mean?

mean(resultOf10rep)

[1] 1.9


If we change the sample size to 1000, what’s the sample mean?

# First time
resultOf1000rep1<-replicate(1000, sum(sample(x, size=n, replace=TRUE)))
mean(resultOf1000rep1)

[1] 1.528

# Re-select the sample
resultOf1000rep2<-replicate(1000, sum(sample(x, size=n, replace=TRUE)))
mean(resultOf1000rep2)

[1] 1.485


Observation: If the sample size is large enough, the sample mean can be a good estimation for the expectation(population mean).


Variance of a Discrete Random Variable
Variance of a random variable is the expected value of a special function (\(g(X) = E[X-E(X)]^2\)) of this random variable, which measures the variability of \(X\) compared to its mean \(E(X)\).
Variance is a measure to quantify the variability/risk. Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable with PMF \(f(x)\). Then the variance of \(X\) is defined as
\[\begin{align*}
\sigma^2 =var(X)  &= E[(X-\mu)^2] = \sum_x (x-\mu)^2f(x)\\
&= E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2 = \sum_x x^2f(x)-\left[\sum_x^2 xf(x)\right]= E(X^2) -\mu^2.
\end{align*}\]

It measures the mean squared distance of observations on \(X\) from its mean.
\(var(X)\) is always non-negative \(var(X)\geq 0\).
\(var(aX) = a^2var(X)\).

Example: Variance of \(X\), the number of heads tossing a fair coin 3 times is \[\begin{align*}
    \sigma^2 =E(X^2)-\mu^2 & = \sum_x^2 xf(x) - \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2\\
    &= 0^2\cdot \frac{1}{8} + 1^2 \cdot \frac{3}{8} + 2^2\cdot \frac{3}{8} + 3^2\cdot \frac{1}{8} -\frac{9}{4} = \frac{3}{4}.
\end{align*}\]


Using R to calculate the sample variance
What are the sample variance?

var(resultOf10rep)

[1] 0.3222222

var(resultOf1000rep1)

[1] 0.7239399

var(resultOf1000rep2)

[1] 0.7445195


Observation: If the sample size is large enough, the sample variance can be a good estimation for (population) variance.

the number of observations;
the number of attributes;
variable types;
missing values, if any; and
any data cleaning, preprocessing, or transformations performed.

Conduct exploratory data analysis to understand the important characteristics and relationships in your dataset.
Your analysis must include at least:

one histogram;
one boxplot; and
one overlay histogram.

Additional visualizations and descriptive statistics are encouraged when appropriate.

Conduct at least one hypothesis test.
You should:

clearly state the null and alternative hypotheses;
select an appropriate statistical test;
explain why the test is appropriate; and
interpret the result in the context of your research question.



4. Linear Regression

Your analysis should:

identify significant predictors;
assess the fitted model;
use the model to predict the response for a test dataset; and
evaluate the prediction results.
